Editors' Note

The editors wish to thank Professor Grünbaum for his exposé of the defects in the experimental procedures of traditional psychoanalysts in their efforts to reconstruct the patient's past in search of the traumatic causes of current incapacities. We concur also with his description of Freud as an intuitive genius and agree that his intuitions may be more valuable than the cause-effect conclusions drawn from these intuitions. We wish only to add that modern psychoanalysis has moved away from the reconstruction of the past that occupied early analysis (and still preoccupies many analysts loyal to that tradition). Rather, it has learned how to use the intuitions of the analyst and experimental procedures in the psychoanalytic setting.

Modern psychoanalysis has come to recognize that not all characterological structures or symptoms can be explained by identifiable trauma from the past. Much is based on genetic and constitutional factors. Energy and the balance of constructive and destructive inclinations may shape the environment rather than result from it. When an integrated ego that can structure a vision of its own history is the goal of treatment, the accuracy of the alleged facts in such a history is secondary to their power to release the creative potential of the individual.

To the extent that Grünbaum remains focused on the conceptions of early Freudian theorists rather than on more recent developments in Freudian analysis, he beats a dead horse that refuses to lie down. He does not see that a new horse eagerly awaits a rider. The very questions that Grünbaum raises may have been answered when modern analysts began to track and to join the patients' perceptions in the spirit of true scientific research.

“The basic assumption is that the brain is the organ of the mind.” This is the starting point of Reiser's volume. He is searching for a “conceptual template” that will bridge the gap between brain and mind. He hopes that classical psychoanalysis will provide this template. The subtitle of the book points to this striving “toward a convergence of psychoanalysis and neurobiology.”

In his Outline of Psycho-Analysis (1940), Freud was directed to the same question:

We know two kinds of things about…our psyche (or mental life): firstly, its bodily organ and scene of action, the brain (or nervous system) and, on the other hand, our acts of consciousness, which are immediate data and cannot be further explained by any sort of description. Everything that lies between is unknown to us…

Freud offered two hypotheses to deal with this problem:

The first is concerned with localization. We assume that mental life is the function of an apparatus to which we ascribe the characteristics of being extended in space and being made up of several portions—which we imagine, that is, as resembling a telescope or microscope or something of this kind.

Mahony pursues here the literary-critical method of studying Freud's texts that he first applied to interesting effect in his Freud as a Writer. The subject of this monograph is, as he makes explicit in a prefatory note, not the “wolf man,” Serge Pankejeff, or whatever cries of his may be referred to in the title, but the text of Freud's great case history, “From The History of an Infantile Neurosis,” among his other writings; and its object is Freud. Much of the considerable ancillary literature on this case is nodded to in passing, and a nicely potted biography of Pankejeff is furnished. But Mahony's eye is captivated by Freud's text, which is what his method is impressively well designed to analyze. Briefly (and necessarily a bit crudely), the patient (that is, the wolf man) as he is dealt with here can be compared to a character in a dream of Freud's being analyzed by a very intelligent and attentive, classical Freudian practitioner. The latent content is painstakingly laid bare and interpreted; inconsistencies are found and accounted for; puns are discovered; etc. It is Freud who is being analyzed—always a worthwhile pastime. Mahony is, as earlier, very hard on Strachey's translations. Of course, criticism of any translation is another worthwhile pastime, given the inherent imperfectibility of that art; but Mahony comes to seem highhanded, and ungrateful for Strachey's great, inevitably flawed, achievement. Nevertheless Mahony's own contribution to Freud studies, his particular literary-critical methodology, is by no means negligible or unworthy of gratitude in its turn.

To say that every one of Freud's words has become enshrined is no longer an exaggeration. Through computer technology it is now possible to locate any word at all that Freud used, as these have been translated into English. This magnificent Concordance lists each word in the Standard Edition (excluding “the”, “and”, etc.), gives a frequency count of its occurrence, the phrase in which it occurs, title of the work in which it appears, and the original date of publication.

Such a work is both an aid to further study and testimony to the continuing influence of the thinker whose words are still being pondered by psychoanalysts, intellectual historians, and philosophers. This Concordance will most certainly be of help to anyone wishing to cite Freud, to recall just where some dimly remembered quotation occurred, or to try to comprehend his full significance.

A work in the philosophy of science, albeit using Freud to argue the virtues of “eliminative inductivism” over “falsificationism” of Karl Popper, may seem as far from the clinical concerns of psychoanalysis as a book about psychoanalysis could be. And yet, if treatment and research are as interdependent as analysts, following Freud, generally claim, it behooves them to become aware of Adolf Grünbaum's thorough criticism of Freud's claim to have justified his theories by means of evidence obtained from patients in the psychoanalytic dialogue.

In The Foundations of Psychoanalysis, Grünbaum takes psychoanalysis at its word in treating it as a natural science whose hypotheses must be empirically confirmed. If one wishes to call it a social or behavioral science that is no matter, unless one means that it is a hermeneutic or humanistic science. Hermeneutic philosophers such as Habermas and Ricoeur have argued that the data of human affairs have a different relation to their subject than do those of other sciences, being related as meanings rather than as causally connected events. These thinkers are unusual in their relation to Freud's work because they regard their criticism as a rehabilitation of it; i.e., they regard what he says as true, so long as it is properly understood and in particular is separated from his mechanistic metapsychology. Marie Cardinal is a well-known contemporary French novelist, author of ten novels, a prominent feminist and a familiar and sought-after media figure. Her first novel, Ecoutez La Mer (1962) won the “Prix International”. Her sixth, The Words To Say It, won “Le Prix Littlé” (1976), an award given annually for the best medical arts book published in France. It has been translated into 18 languages, appearing in English in 1983.

It is the story of a seven-year long psychoanalysis which turns out to be entirely successful. Analysis is the last recourse for this housewife and mother of three children who just had a psychotic break and has been suffering for years from a variety of ailments. She is mostly terrified by continuous menstrual bleeding which no medical intervention can stop, and by powerful anxiety attacks—she calls them “the Thing”—that leave her wailing and cowering in a corner in her bathroom.

Freud's Rules of Dream Interpretation. Alexander Grinstein. New York: International Universities Press, 1983. 306 pp.

June Bernstein

June Bernstein

June Bernstein  

The title of this book accurately describes its contents. Grinstein has collected, from various sources in the Collected Works, the essential rules for working with dreams. The presentation is so accurate and clearly written that it would make an excellent text from which to study for an exam.

In addition to reviewing Freud's rules, Grinstein offers illuminating examples from his own practice to demonstrate how the rules are applied. Although Grinstein warns us that dreams cannot be interpreted without the patient's associations, he shows himself (as did Freud) to be adept at understanding typical dreams as well as the symbols, metaphors, word play and other operations of the dream work. Furthermore, he displays tact and sensitivity in dealing with his patients' dreams. He offers only what the patient can hear without narcissistic injury and is alert to the transference (including the negative transference) meaning. His major aim in dealing with dreams appears to be to elicit more information about the patient's past life and infantile conflicts. Grinstein talks to the patient in an honest, rational and straightforward manner in an appeal to the rational ego; there is no effort to mobilize or resolve resistance through the use of emotional communication.

This book is not innovative, but it performs a valuable service in clearly presenting an up-to-date version of classical dream analysis.

According to Erberwein, psychoanalyst Bertram Lewin introduced the term “dream screen” to refer to a primal screen upon which every individual perceives his own oneiric world. He contends that in viewing films we regress to an infantile state of experience akin to dreaming. As in infancy or in nightly dream states, while watching films, images and other stimuli occur which allow for tension release.

The first part of the book discusses the idea of the dream screen in a theoretical way with emphasis on physiology. In part two, Erberwein discusses scenes from actual films depicting the dreams of leading characters and the special effects which produce dreamlike states, such as voice-overs, fades, dissolves, and superimpositions. There is a very moving discussion of “The Elephant Man” (who is able to survive by holding within him the comfort he associates with his mother)

Editors Introduction

In Autumn, 1984, the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies inaugurated its new group training program with a series of lectures on modern group analysis. The texts of three of the four lectures are published here. Because of a prior commitment, the text of the fourth lecture, by Louis Ormont, will be published by a different journal.

The distinctive clinical and theoretical viewpoint of modern psychoanalysis makes the phenomena surrounding the subject of group analysis a focus of attention in the training of students. Powerful emotional forces are released when individuals meet together in groups. In the effective use of these emotional responses lies a special contribution of modern analysis. In these lectures, experienced practitioners discuss and demonstrate a variety of modern methods and approaches to special as well as general problems arising in the practice of group analysis.

Hyman Spotnitz discusses the powerful forces that are generated when people in individual treatment are assembled in groups of as many as twenty or more. Spotnitz demonstrates how the group leader facilitates the expression of these forces and how emotional communication, properly channeled, leads to individual maturation as well as creativity.

Phyllis Meadow's lecture focuses on the shifts and patterns of resistances that appear when marital partners, parents and children, and colleagues join each other in group settings.

Leslie Rosenthal examines how both individual and group resistances manifest themselves over the life of a group and how the resolution of group resistances can facilitate maturation simultaneously among various members.

Editors Introduction

With this issue, Modern Psychoanalysis enters its second decade. The editors are prompted to reflection. It may be time to consider what we've been about, now that a body of evidence has accumulated in the form of eighteen issues totalling some 2600 pages. We began with some aims in mind, and we've kept them in mind—so some retrospection may not be idle—there may be some value in reexamining our purposes, possibly to renew our commitment to them. And then, psychoanalysts never disdain history.

Modern Psychoanalysis, the journal of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies, first appeared in the Spring of 1976, giving as its purposes: To document the movement, then already 20 years in process, to expand the application of psychoanalytic practice beyond the original limits set by Freud; to encourage the publication of papers reporting the development of theory and technique that would finally apply psychoanalytic method to treating the full spectrum of human emotional disorders.

Documenting the ongoing development of modern psychoanalysis has taken many forms, including reports of work in progress in our departments of Research and Experimentation in Psychoanalysis and Applied Psychoanalysis, as well as such finished clinical work as the landmark case report by Evelyn J. Liegner that constituted the whole content of Volume Five, Number One, in 1980. Modern Psychoanalysis has also been pleased to publish from time to time the annual scientific conferencs of the National Association for the Advancement of Psychoanalysis—the papers presented and the discussions they engender—a source both of advance and of broadening the application of analytic methodologies.

In The Structure of Freudian Thought Melvin Feffer makes the case that limitations in Freud's epistemology have created significant logical inconsistencies in his theory of personality development. Feffer provides a thorough overview of Freud's various theories of development. He then describes the inconsistencies that he finds in each of them. He argues that they are all related, and states that they are indicative of “the problem of immutability and discontinuity” (p. 41).

This problem is complex. It is most clearly illustrated in Feffer's analysis of the evolution of the pleasure principle into the reality principle. According to one of Freud's accounts, the primitive personality consists solely of impulses striving for discharge. The ability to delay gratification develops as these impulses are frustrated by reality. Drawing on the work of Hartmann and White, Feffer points out that if there is nothing in the personality except these impulses, then there is nothing there which could develop the capacity to delay gratification. Freud makes the reality principle appear out of nothing—as if by magic. This leap in development, whereby structures appear in the psyche as if out of nothing, is what Feffer calls the problem of discontinuity.

Are Freudian slips in trouble? The answer is yes to Daniel Goleman (1984) who reviewed a few of the recent psychological studies and interviewed several writers in this field. Goleman says: “Freud read hidden meanings in every slip. But the new school of thought holds that the vast majority of slips are devoid of ulterior motives or meanings; though some may, indeed, be motivated by unconscious conflicts, more often than not, a slip is just a slip” (p. C1).

On the other hand, Charles Brenner takes a more optimistic view. According to Brenner, the trouble with this new school of thought is that its proponents do not use the psychoanalytical method to test Freud's hypothesis. If they did, “A hidden determinant would be found even for the most seemingly innocuous slips” (Brenner, in Goleman, 1984).

The topic of resistance in groups and group resistance was memorialized some years ago in a cartoon in The New Yorker which shows two gentleman of rather shabby leisure conversing on a park bench. The caption reads, “For heaven's sake, I'm a group therapy dropout, too.” That cartoon sits on my desk as a reminder of the omnipresence of resistance and also of the omnipresent inadequacy of group therapists.

I looked at the cartoon recently and realized that one of the characters bore a resemblance to a person who left one of my groups, a gentleman who had come in under considerable pressure from his wife because he had such a bad relationship with their daughter. In the initial interview he told me he had had treatment before, ten sessions with an analyst. I introduced him to the group by saying, “This is John and you all better get to know him pretty quickly because he's not going to be around much longer.” John protested the unfairness of this comment. In his second session he told the group how he handled his daughter, and they gave him all kinds of good advice which he went home and carried out. Ten sessions later he bade a happy farewell to the group.

Resistance was first mentioned almost a hundred years ago by its discoverer, Sigmund Freud (1895). From the publication of Studies in Hysteria onward, the concept evolved and was clarified. In the beginning it was seen as an action taken by the ego to protect the process of repression, and the analyst's task was to overcome it. It was “nothing but the child's character” and stood in the way of analytic work (1897, p. 226).

In this volume, Rothstein argues against the necessity for replacing Freud's structural hypothesis by a radically new model of

the mind. He believes that if we take an evolutionary perspective about the development of mental structure, we will have little dificulty in integrating new data with traditional metapsychology. For instance, we may consider that the child is capable of intrand intersystemic conflict concerning oral and anal sadistic urges without supposing that the conflicts have any relation to those of the phallic-oedipal stage of development. Both ego and superego may be seen as continually developing with roots in the distant past.

This is a fascinating book that should be of special interest to modern analysts because of the emphasis it places on narcissistic injury in the genesis of symptoms, dreams and character disorders. Rothstein equates narcissism with the felt quality of perfection, and narcissistic injury with its loss. He believes that the loss of the self-object bliss of the symbiotic phase is an insult from which few of us ever recover. He draws attention to Freud's idea (in Beyond the Pleasure Principle) that, prior to the establishment of the pleasure principle, the function of dreams is to assimilate traumas that have overwhelmed the stimulus barrier. Rothstein notes that the immature, psychic apparatus is organized beyond the pleasure principle, and that therefore many dreams reflect attempts to assimilate the narcissistic injuries of the dream day—injuries which resonate with the unassimilated narcissistic injuries of childhood. More evolved parts of the ego, pursuing the pleasure (or reality) principles, still have to struggle with archaic counterparts organized beyond the pleasure principle.

In a chapter devoted to understanding how the masochist fits into this evolutionary perspective, Rothstein suggests that the young child's perception of the mother as enraged or sadistic is a profound narcissistic injury. One from of defense against feeling this injury is to identify with the attacking object and to impose pain on the self. This maneuver allows some discharge of aggression, albeit against, the self. Masochism is also (here Rothstein is quoting Berliner) ‘a pathologic way of loving a person who gives hate and ill treatment.’ Although Rothstein finds real deprivation in the history of the masochist, he is aware that mosochism also functions as a defense against aggression toward the object.

In recent decades psychoanalysis has paid increasing attention to the emotional reactions and attitudes of the analyst in the psychoanalytic relationship, and to the role of the analyst as a real object. There is no “normal” emotional state for the therapist, as Racker (1968) emphasized: his inner state is continually and profoundly responsive to the patient and to what the patient is saying and doing.

The vicissitudes of life will of course influence the analyst. There are many factors in the analyst's life situation that can interfere with his ability to attend to the patient in an analytic mode. Faced with the terminal illness and death of my mother, I experienced the hazards of being human along with those of being an analyst. Dynamics of the patient and the analyst, transference and countertransference must all be examined in light of terminal illness and death. A single man who wanted to work with a woman so he could be prepared for marriage entered one of my groups ten years ago. He said he wanted to learn to express anger. During the first sessions he seemed to express nothing else. He complained about what was said and he ranted about what was not said. He spoke of the group members as wrong and stupid and of the analyst as the worst of all. Group members were puzzled by his repetitiveness, but when they asked about this venting of spleen, he expressed surprise. “What else would a successful group member do?” Within several weeks he recognized that other kinds of communication were taking place in the group. Like this man, many people come to group with preconceived notions. Some think that it's for people who are shy or need help in socializing. Analytic candidates may come to round out their training. We do not, ordinarily, think of the feeling of death as contagious. Infectious diseases are, of course, transmissible through a virus, and contagious through contact with an organism carrying the virus.

Psychoanalytic researchers have borrowed the concept from biology, and became interested in the contagion of feelings. Escalona (1953) points to the mother/infant dyad and shows the extreme susceptibility of one to the other of emotions. Spotnitz and Meadow (1976) elaborate on the idea, and extend it to the emotional communication that takes place in the analytic setting between patient and analyst.

Death seems different, though. Death comes in varied sizes and shapes. In the absence of a known physical entity that serves as an infectious agent, we do not think that we must die merely because something else has. The idea of death doesn't seem to be catching.

Yet, there is some evidence that seems to belie our sense that each impulse toward death is independent of every other impulse toward death. The recent phenomenon of teen-age suicide has the look of an infectious disease. Clusters of deaths are occurring. Apparently once one occurs, another is more likely, and yet another, until it begins to have the look of an epidemic.

A psychoanalytic group that I have been running for a little over a year gives evidence of the phenomenological sense of death as contagious. The group was an already established cancer group that. I inherited.

Introduction

Defenses serve to protect the ego from conscious awareness of unacceptable thoughts and feelings associated with the sexual and aggressive drives. One of the contributions of modern psychoanalysis to the understanding of severe emotional pathology, including psychosomatic states, is its conceptualization of the narcissistic defense. The regressed patient, who fears that his aggression will obliterate the object on whom he depends for narcissistic supplies, protects the object by invoking the narcissistic defense, in which his aggressive impulses are turned inward upon his psychological and/or physical self (Spotnitz, 1969).

The case of Virginia Seton illustrates how three seemingly diverse symptoms—acne, hallucinations, and systematized religious thought—were related in being complementary manifestations of the narcissistic defense. The psychosomatic component exemplifies the turning of aggression onto the self in an attack on one's own body, and the choice of organ provides a clue in determining the period of development at which the conflict arose. The schizophrenic component, consisting of both auditory and cenesthetic hallucinations (sensations arising from bodily organs), illustrates not only the damage that can be done to the thought processes and perceptual apparatus by turning aggression back upon the mind, but also the disguised, fantasy wish-fulfillment that can be accomplished in the process.

Introduction

This paper derives from two related interests, one personal and one clinical. The primary basis of my long term interest was tied to personal history and concerns with abandonment. Early and continuous experiences with being left engendered a chronic expectation in my work with patients that they were also preparing to leave me.

Along with the fear that I would be left was the expectation that I deserved it because I was such an incompetent therapist and did so many things wrong or incorrectly. When I first became interested in this topic, the thought that relationships might be maintained with me in spite of my errors was emotionally impossible for me to accept. Such a transference to my patients often meant I was distracted from their messages to me by my own panicky responses to perceived threats of termination.

The topic of premature termination of treatment has an important place in the history of psychoanalysis.

If psychoanalysis is to have a viable future it must be changed and developed on the basis of observation and experimentation and not be viewed as a body of fixed principles. This principle of empirical science is emphasized by the editor in this Festchrift in honor of Heinz Kohut, the originator of self-psychology, possibly neglecting the role played by the kind of creative theory formation exemplified by Kohut's work.

Classical psychoanalysis views neurotic relatedness as a response to oedipal drive conflicts. In treatment the transference neurosis is a reenactment of the maladaptive responses to an unresolved Oedipus complex which can be resolved by interpretation. In the narcissistic neuroses, however, the patient relates to the analyst in another way. The narcissistic patient may feel dead and empty and lack affect, view the analyst as omnipotent or worthless and experience the analyst like those parts of himself of which he is unaware. Most modern analysts regard the patient's difficulties as the product of unresolved drive conflicts experienced during the pre-oedipal period. Kohut also sees the patient as being damaged primarily during the pre-oedipal period, but regards his difficulties as a result of “missing narcissistic structures” rather than as defenses against conflicting drives. Kohut postulates a “cohesive self” for the mature adult. The self, according to Kohut, matures and develops in response to appropriate empathic affective responses from the parents. For example, when the child is in an early omnipotent phase the appropriate affective response would be pleasure in the childs's expressions of grandiosity. The perception of parental affective communication teaches the child what he is feeling and builds structures of the self. The calming, soothing function of the mother, for example, is incorporated into the self and promotes object constancy.

The Origins of Psychoanalysis—the edited selection of Freud's letters to Fliess—proved to be informative but tantalizing. It certainly provided an exciting picture of Freud's mind at work during his most creative period, but the knowledge that portions of the letters had been omitted left one unsatisfied. Although the editors' wish to protect Freud's personal and professional confidences is understandable (especially in light of Freud's initial wish that the letters be destroyed), it was not credible that the letters that were deemed “confidential” contained nothing of significance. Ernest Jones and Max Schur, both of whom had access to the letters, confirmed these suspicions when they included important passages from the unpublished letters in their biographical works.

The guardians of Freud's legacy kept the complete correspondence shrouded in the same secrecy that surrounds The Freud Archives until Jeffrey Masson succeeded in persuading Anna Freud to permit their publication.
